scenarios.title: The clinic's three promises
scenarios.situation: A small clinic asks you what information security means for their patient records. The manager wants one plain-language explanation they can share with staff.
scenarios.prompt: Which explanation correctly maps the CIA triad?
choices: Confidentiality means the records are backed up, integrity means they are encrypted, availability means everyone can see them
Confidentiality, integrity, and availability are three brands of firewall
Confidentiality means only authorized staff see the records, integrity means the records are not altered, availability means the systems work when patients arrive
The triad only applies to hospitals, not small clinics
scenarios.why: Confidentiality protects information from unauthorized eyes, integrity protects it from unauthorized change, and availability keeps it usable when needed. The three words are a checklist: for any system, ask who should see it, whether it could be tampered with, and whether it will be there when needed.
scenarios.hint: Match each word to its plain meaning: secret, unaltered, reachable.

scenarios.title: Two proofs are better than one
scenarios.situation: A new employee logs in with a password, then taps approve on a prompt sent to their phone. A coworker says that is two-factor authentication; another says it is just logging in twice.
scenarios.prompt: Who is right, and why?
choices: The first coworker — the password is something you know and the phone is something you have: two different factor types
The second coworker — typing a password and tapping a phone are the same thing done twice
Neither — multi-factor requires three factors minimum
Both — the terms mean the same thing
scenarios.why: Authentication factors are categories: something you know (password), something you have (phone, token), something you are (fingerprint). Multi-factor means combining different categories, so stealing one is not enough. A password plus a password hint is still one factor.
scenarios.hint: Count the categories of proof, not the number of steps.

scenarios.title: The stolen password that went nowhere
scenarios.situation: An attacker buys a user's password from a breach dump and tries it on the company portal. The login fails because the portal also requires approving a push notification on the user's phone.
scenarios.prompt: Why did multi-factor authentication stop the attacker?
choices: The second factor is something the attacker does not have — a correct password alone is no longer enough
The password was too short for the attacker to type correctly
Breach dumps never contain real passwords
The portal was offline during the attack
scenarios.why: Passwords leak constantly through breaches, phishing, and reuse. MFA adds a second, independent proof — usually possession of a device — so a stolen password alone cannot complete the login. It is the single highest-value control most organizations can deploy.
scenarios.hint: What did the attacker have, and what were they missing?

scenarios.title: The lock anyone can close
scenarios.situation: A job applicant needs to send sensitive documents to a hiring manager securely. The manager publishes a public key and keeps a private key secret.
scenarios.prompt: How should the applicant protect the documents?
choices: Encrypt with the manager's private key, which the manager should share first
The public key decrypts, so send the documents in the clear and share the public key separately
Public and private keys are identical, so either one works for everything
Encrypt with the manager's public key — only the manager's private key can open them
scenarios.why: In asymmetric cryptography the keys are a matched pair with opposite jobs: the public key encrypts (anyone can lock), the private key decrypts (only the owner can open). The public key is shared freely; the private key is never shared. That is what makes secure communication with strangers possible.
scenarios.hint: Which key is safe to publish, and what job does each key do?

scenarios.title: The breached database with no passwords in it
scenarios.situation: A website is breached and its user database is stolen. The attackers find passwords stored as salted hashes, not plain text, and cannot log in as users.
scenarios.prompt: Why do systems store hashes instead of the actual passwords?
choices: Hashes are faster to type than passwords
Hashes make passwords impossible for users to forget
Hashing lets the system verify a password without storing the secret itself — a stolen database does not hand over the passwords
Storing plain text is illegal everywhere, so hashes are the only option
scenarios.why: A hash is a one-way fingerprint: the system hashes what you type and compares it to the stored hash, so the real password never sits in the database. When (not if) the database leaks, attackers get fingerprints they cannot reverse into passwords. Salting adds uniqueness so identical passwords hash differently.
scenarios.hint: What does the system actually compare when you log in?

scenarios.title: The window left open
scenarios.situation: A ground-floor office window does not lock. The neighborhood has seen several break-ins recently. The office manager asks whether this is actually a security risk worth fixing.
scenarios.prompt: What is the risk here, and what reduces it most directly?
choices: There is no risk — windows are not IT equipment
The risk is the window itself; remove all windows
Only the break-in statistics matter; the window is irrelevant
The risk is the chance that the threat (burglars) exploits the vulnerability (unlocked window); locking or securing the window reduces it
scenarios.why: Risk is the potential that a threat exploits a vulnerability to cause harm. The threat is the burglar, the vulnerability is the unlocked window, and the risk is the combination. You reduce risk by addressing either side — remove the vulnerability (lock the window) or reduce the threat — and the cheapest effective fix usually targets the vulnerability.
scenarios.hint: Name the threat, name the weakness, then see how they combine.

scenarios.title: The intern with the master key
scenarios.situation: To make onboarding easier, IT gives a new intern full administrator access to every system on day one. The intern only needs email and the shared drive.
scenarios.prompt: What principle does this violate, and what is the danger?
choices: Availability — the intern will slow the systems down
Encryption — the intern's laptop is not encrypted
Least privilege — grant only the access needed for the job; extra access magnifies both mistakes and breaches
No principle — more access is always better for productivity
scenarios.why: Least privilege means every person and process gets the minimum access needed — nothing more. An intern with admin rights can accidentally (or maliciously) cause damage far beyond their role, and if their account is compromised, the attacker inherits the keys to everything. Start small; add access only with justification.
scenarios.hint: What happens when this account — or its mistakes — gets more power than the job needs?

scenarios.title: The bakery that baked through ransomware
scenarios.situation: A bakery's order computer is hit by ransomware and every file is encrypted. The owner plugs in an external drive that is normally kept unplugged in a drawer, restores the files, and is taking orders again by lunch.
scenarios.prompt: What saved the bakery, and what made the backup trustworthy?
choices: Luck — ransomware usually decrypts itself after a few hours
Offline backups plus a restore plan — the drive was disconnected so the malware could not reach it, and the owner knew how to restore
The antivirus — it silently fixed everything
Paying the ransom quickly — the attackers sent the key
scenarios.why: Backups only save you if the disaster cannot reach them: an offline or disconnected copy survives ransomware that encrypts everything on the network. And a backup you have never restored is a rumor — the owner had practiced the restore, so recovery took hours instead of weeks.
scenarios.hint: Why didn't the ransomware encrypt the external drive too?

scenarios.title: Four hours or the wedding cakes do not ship
scenarios.situation: A bakery manager tells IT: if the order system is down more than four hours, the day's revenue is lost — and they can afford to lose at most one hour of entered orders.
scenarios.prompt: What are these two requirements called?
choices: RTO of four hours (how fast it must be back) and RPO of one hour (how much data loss is tolerable)
RPO of four hours and RTO of one hour — time and data are the same thing
An SLA and a password policy
Two ways of saying the system must never fail
scenarios.why: Recovery Time Objective (RTO) is how long the business can survive without the system; Recovery Point Objective (RPO) is how much data it can afford to lose, which sets how often backups must run. The business states them, IT builds recovery to meet them.
scenarios.hint: Which number is about the clock, and which is about the data?

scenarios.title: Do not pull the plug just yet
scenarios.situation: An employee sees a malware alert on their PC and is about to wipe the machine completely to get back to work. A coworker stops them and says to call IT first.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct first response, and why not wipe immediately?
choices: Wipe it — speed matters more than anything
Ignore the alert — antivirus handles everything silently
Disconnect from the network, leave the machine on, and report it — wiping destroys evidence of how the malware arrived and whether it spread
Email the malware to a friend to get a second opinion
scenarios.why: The first move in incident response is containment: disconnect the machine so the malware cannot spread, while preserving the system for investigation. Wiping first destroys the evidence that shows how the infection happened — and whether other machines are infected too. Report, contain, then let the response process decide.
scenarios.hint: If you wipe it, what questions can nobody ever answer?

scenarios.title: The plan for the people vs the plan for the computers
scenarios.situation: A burst pipe floods the office. Staff need somewhere to work on Monday, and the servers need to be brought back online. The manager pulls out two plans: the BCP and the DRP.
scenarios.prompt: What is the difference between the two plans?
choices: They are identical — the names are interchangeable
The BCP is for computers and the DRP is for people
Only large companies need either plan
The business continuity plan keeps the business running (alternate site, communications, key processes); the disaster recovery plan restores the IT systems
scenarios.why: Business continuity is about the business: where people work, how customers are served, which processes matter most. Disaster recovery is the IT subset: restoring servers, data, and networks. DRP feeds into BCP — technology recovery serves business survival, not the other way around.
scenarios.hint: Which plan cares about where the staff sit on Monday?

scenarios.title: The drill with no computers
scenarios.situation: The office team sits around a conference table and talks through what everyone would do if a flood hit the building. No systems are touched; it is all discussion.
scenarios.prompt: What is the value of this exercise?
choices: None — only real disasters teach anything
It tests the plan and everyone's role cheaply: gaps in contacts, responsibilities, and decisions surface before a real crisis
It replaces the need for backups
It is a team-building lunch with extra steps
scenarios.why: A tabletop exercise walks the team through a scenario verbally, revealing the gaps paper plans hide: outdated phone numbers, unclear decision authority, steps nobody owns. It costs an afternoon and finds the flaws while there is still time to fix them — which is the whole point of testing plans.
scenarios.hint: What is cheaper: finding the gap in a meeting, or during the flood?

scenarios.title: The laptop that might be evidence
scenarios.situation: A manager suspects a departing employee copied customer lists to a company laptop. IT is asked to examine it, and someone suggests just reimaging it quickly to reassign it.
scenarios.prompt: What must the team NOT do, and why?
choices: Do not wipe, reimage, or keep using the laptop — altering it destroys potential evidence of what was taken
Do not tell the manager — investigations should be secret from everyone
Do not document anything — paperwork slows investigations
There are no restrictions; reimage it immediately
scenarios.why: Once a device may hold evidence, every change to it — wiping, reinstalling, even browsing — can destroy proof of what happened and when. The correct move is to stop using it, secure it, document who handles it, and let the investigation process run. Evidence you alter is evidence you lose.
scenarios.hint: If this becomes a legal matter, what will lawyers ask about the laptop's history?

scenarios.title: The meeting after the mess
scenarios.situation: After a painful day-long outage, the team holds a meeting to discuss what went wrong and what to change. One person worries it will turn into a blame session.
scenarios.prompt: What is the purpose of this meeting, and how should it be run?
choices: To assign blame so people work harder next time
A blameless review to improve the plan and controls so the failure does not repeat — focus on process, not people
To decide who gets fired
There is no purpose; outages are unavoidable
scenarios.why: The lessons-learned (post-incident) review exists to convert a painful event into durable improvements: fix the plan, add the missing control, update the runbook. Blame makes people hide mistakes; a blameless focus on process gets honest answers — and honest answers are what prevent the repeat.
scenarios.hint: Do you want people to hide their mistakes, or report them?

scenarios.title: The backup that was encrypted too
scenarios.situation: Ransomware hits. The team reaches for backups — and finds the backup server encrypted as well: it was on the same network, with the same admin credentials, writable from the compromised domain.
evidence: Field observation
Observed: Ransomware hits. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
What 'done' looks like

Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Design ransomware-proof backups (2) Apply 3-2-1 with immutability Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What backup architecture survives ransomware?
choices: A. More frequent backups to the same server; frequency is the fix.

B. 3-2-1 with immutability and isolation: 3 copies, 2 media/locations, 1 offline or immutable (object-locked, air-gapped, or separate credentials) — the backup must not be writable from the environment it protects, and restores must be tested.
C. Backups to the cloud; the cloud cannot be encrypted.
D. One backup is enough if it is recent.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the attackers encrypted the backup with the same credentials. What separated the backup from production — nothing? Fix that.
scenarios.why: Ransomware hunts backups first — modern variants enumerate network shares and backup servers before encrypting. A backup reachable with the same credentials over the same network is not a backup; it is a second victim. 3-2-1 is the baseline (3 copies, 2 different media/locations, 1 offsite), but the ransomware era adds the critical qualifier: the offsite copy must be immutable (object-locked/WORM so nothing — not even admin credentials — can alter it within retention) or offline/air-gapped. And per the control-testing lesson: the restore is the control, tested regularly. Cloud copies (choice C) are encryptable too if the keys are reachable.

scenarios.title: The SLA the business actually needs
scenarios.situation: IT promises 'we will recover everything in 4 hours with zero data loss.' The business never agreed to the cost of that promise — and during an outage, the business actually needed email in 1 hour but could wait a week for the analytics warehouse.
evidence: Field observation

Observed: IT promises 'we will recover everything in 4 hours with zero data loss.' The business never agreed to the cost of that promise — and during an outage, the business actually needed email in 1 hour but could wait a week for the analytics warehouse. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
What 'done' looks like

Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Derive RTO/RPO from a BIA (2) Tier recovery by business impact Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct RTO/RPO discipline?
choices: A. Promise 4 hours / zero loss for everything; ambition is good.

B. Derive RTO (max tolerable downtime) and RPO (max tolerable data loss) PER SYSTEM from a Business Impact Analysis with business owners — then engineer (and fund) recovery to those targets. Different systems get different targets; the targets are business decisions with price tags.
C. Let IT set RTO/RPO; the business does not understand recovery.
D. Set RTO/RPO once and never revisit; stability matters.
scenarios.hint: Hint: who feels the pain of downtime — IT, or the business? Who should set the target?
scenarios.why: RTO/RPO are business decisions disguised as technical targets: only the business owner can say 'email down 4 hours costs $X' — and only with that number can IT price the recovery architecture (hot standby vs nightly backups) and ask whether the target is worth it. The BIA (Business Impact Analysis) is the process: interview owners, quantify downtime cost over time, set per-system RTO/RPO, get sign-off. Uniform promises (choice A) either overspend on the warehouse or underserve email — usually both. IT-set targets (choice C) optimize for engineering comfort, not business need.

scenarios.title: The drill where everyone looked at IT
scenarios.situation: The tabletop exercise begins: 'Ransomware has encrypted the file servers.' Everyone turns to the IT manager. Legal, comms, and the executives have no idea what they are supposed to do — the plan never assigned them roles.
evidence: Field observation

Observed: The tabletop exercise begins: 'Ransomware has encrypted the file servers.' Everyone turns to the IT manager. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
What 'done' looks like

Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Facilitate tabletop exercises (2) Convert findings to plan updates Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What makes a tabletop exercise actually work?
choices: A. More technical detail; the scenario was too simple.

B. Cross-functional participation with assigned roles, a facilitator who injects complications (backups also hit, press calls, ransom note), and a focus on DECISIONS and handoffs — the exercise tests the plan and the people, especially the non-IT parts everyone skipped.
C. Only IT needs to drill; others just slow it down.
D. Tabletops are obsolete; real incidents are the drill.
scenarios.hint: Hint: everyone looked at IT. What had the plan failed to give everyone else?
scenarios.why: Tabletops test the plan, not the technology: the value is discovering that legal does not know the breach-notification timeline, comms has no holding statement, and the executive has never seen the plan — BEFORE the incident. The facilitator's injections (backups compromised, press calling, ransom demand with a deadline) force the decisions the plan glosses over: do we pay? who decides? who talks to whom, in what order? IT-only drills (choice C) rehearse the one part that already gets exercised; the exercise in the scenario failed precisely where IT-only preparation always fails — the handoffs. Real incidents (choice D) are the most expensive possible drill.

scenarios.title: The new hire's first day
scenarios.situation: HR enters a new employee as an accountant in the identity system, and the correct email, file shares, and finance apps are provisioned automatically based on that role.
scenarios.prompt: What access control model is this?
choices: Discretionary access control — the employee decides their own access
Role-based access control — permissions are assigned to the role, and people inherit them by being in the role
Mandatory access control — the government assigned a clearance level
No model — this is just convenience
scenarios.why: Role-based access control (RBAC) ties permissions to job roles rather than individuals: join the accountant role, get accountant access; change roles, and access follows automatically. It scales far better than hand-crafting permissions per person, and it makes reviews simple — audit the role, not every user.
scenarios.hint: What did HR actually assign — permissions, or a job title that carries permissions?

scenarios.title: The folder owner shares
scenarios.situation: A team lead shares their project folder with a contractor for two weeks, choosing exactly which files the contractor can open.
scenarios.prompt: What model lets the data owner make that call?
choices: Mandatory access control — the system administrator must approve every share
Role-based access control — only the contractor role can be shared
No control — sharing is always insecure
Discretionary access control — the owner of the resource decides who gets access
scenarios.why: Discretionary access control (DAC) puts the owner in charge: the person who owns the file or folder decides who may access it. It is flexible and familiar — it is how most file sharing works — but it relies on owners making good decisions, which is why sensitive data usually needs stronger models.
scenarios.hint: Who made the sharing decision — a policy, or the person who owns the folder?

scenarios.title: The stamp that decides
scenarios.situation: Government documents carry labels like Confidential and Secret. The system compares each user's clearance to each document's label and grants or denies access automatically — no user can override it.
scenarios.prompt: What model is this?
choices: Mandatory access control — the system enforces access from security labels; users cannot change the rules
Discretionary — the document authors choose the readers
Role-based — everyone with the same job sees the same files
Voluntary — access is optional
scenarios.why: Mandatory access control (MAC) is system-enforced: labels on data (classification) and labels on users (clearance) decide access, and no user discretion can override them. It is strict and inflexible — which is exactly what environments with classified information require.
scenarios.hint: Can the document owner share it with a friend anyway? That is the test.

scenarios.title: The cashier who also approves refunds
scenarios.situation: One retail employee can both issue refunds and approve them. Last month, fake refunds totaling $9,000 went to an accomplice's account before anyone noticed.
scenarios.prompt: What control would have prevented a single person from doing this?
choices: Longer passwords for the cashier
More security cameras
A faster refund process
Separation of duties — split the task so issuing and approving require two different people; fraud then needs collusion
scenarios.why: Separation of duties divides sensitive tasks so no single person controls a process end to end. One person issuing and another approving means fraud requires two people conspiring — far rarer and far easier to detect. It is a people-and-process control, not a technology purchase.
scenarios.hint: How many people had to agree for the fraud to work? How many should it take?

scenarios.title: The friendly stranger with the coffee
scenarios.situation: An employee badges into the office and a stranger carrying two coffee cups follows them through the door, smiling and saying thanks. The stranger has no badge visible.
scenarios.prompt: What should the employee do?
choices: Politely stop them and direct them to reception to sign in and get a visitor badge — tailgating is a classic intrusion method
Hold the door — it is polite, and the coffee cups prove they work here
Ignore it — physical security is the guards' problem
Take a photo and post it online
scenarios.why: Tailgating (piggybacking) is one of the oldest intrusion techniques: follow an authorized person through a controlled door. The defense is cultural — every employee enforces the badge rule, politely but firmly, and visitors go through reception. Politeness is the attacker's tool; procedure is yours.
scenarios.hint: What is the attacker counting on you feeling?

scenarios.title: The account that outlived the employee
scenarios.situation: An employee left six months ago, but their account was never disabled. An attacker found the stale credentials in an old breach dump and used them to log in last week.
scenarios.prompt: What process failed, and what is the fix?
choices: Provisioning — accounts were created too slowly
Deprovisioning — accounts must be disabled promptly when people leave; tie it to the HR departure process
Encryption — the account was not encrypted
Backup — the account was not backed up
scenarios.why: Deprovisioning removes access when it is no longer needed — departures, role changes, contractors ending. Stale accounts are attacker favorites: nobody watches them, and their passwords never change. The fix is procedural: HR triggers IT on every departure, and access reviews catch what the process misses.
scenarios.hint: When should the account's life have ended?

scenarios.title: The curious coworker
scenarios.situation: An employee asks IT for a peek at a colleague's salary file, saying they are just curious and promise not to tell anyone.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct response?
choices: Share it — curiosity is harmless and they promised secrecy
Share it but ask them not to copy it
Post the salaries publicly so nobody has to ask
Deny the request — access requires a business need-to-know, not curiosity; even authorized staff only see what their job requires
scenarios.why: Need-to-know (a facet of least privilege) means access follows job necessity, not curiosity or seniority. Granting one-off peeks trains the organization that access rules are negotiable — and every exception is a precedent. The answer is a polite, firm no, with the request logged.
scenarios.hint: Does their job require this information?

scenarios.title: The 400 roles nobody understands
scenarios.situation: The company has 400 roles, most with one member, names like 'Temp_Access_2019.' Nobody knows what any role grants. New hires get 'the same as Sarah,' inheriting Sarah's accumulated 6 years of access.
evidence: Field observation

Observed: The company has 400 roles, most with one member, names like 'Temp_Access_2019.' Nobody knows what any role grants. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
What 'done' looks like
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Engineer RBAC roles (2) Stop privilege creep Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct RBAC approach?
choices: A. Keep adding roles; granularity is security.

B. Role engineering: define a small set of job-function roles (least privilege per function), name them clearly, review them regularly, and provision by role — never by cloning another user. 400 mystery roles get consolidated or deleted.
C. Give everyone admin; roles are overhead.
D. Delete all roles and start over every January.
scenarios.hint: Hint: what does role #247 grant? If nobody knows, what is the role FOR?
scenarios.why: RBAC works when roles model job functions: 'Accounts Payable Clerk' grants exactly what AP clerks need — defined once, assigned many times, reviewed periodically. 400 single-member roles are not RBAC; they are per-user permissions wearing role costumes, with all the unmanageability of direct assignment. 'Same as Sarah' cloning is the classic privilege-creep vector: Sarah's 6 years of role changes (never revoked) become the new hire's starting point. The fix is role engineering: mine actual access patterns, define the minimal role set, consolidate, and provision new hires to roles — with regular recertification pruning the drift.

scenarios.title: The help-desk code that bypassed MFA
scenarios.situation: MFA is deployed — but the help desk can reset it with just a name and employee ID, no verification. Attackers social-engineer the desk, reset MFA on executive accounts, and walk in.
evidence: Field observation

Observed: MFA is deployed — but the help desk can reset it with just a name and employee ID, no verification. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
What 'done' looks like
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Deploy MFA correctly (2) Harden the recovery flow Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct MFA program?
choices: A. MFA is deployed; the help-desk process is out of scope.

B. MFA plus a hardened recovery process: strong identity verification for resets (in-person or verified out-of-band), limited break-glass accounts with monitoring, phishing-resistant factors (FIDO2/WebAuthn) for high-risk users — the recovery flow is part of the MFA system, and attackers target the weakest link.
C. Remove MFA; the bypass proves it does not work.
D. SMS codes for everyone; simplest is best.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the attackers never touched the MFA cryptography. What did they attack instead?
scenarios.why: MFA's strength is the strength of its weakest path — and the recovery/reset flow IS part of the system. Attackers do not break cryptography; they call the help desk. The program: phishing-resistant factors where it matters (FIDO2/WebAuthn security keys — immune to credential phishing, unlike SMS/TOTP codes which can be phished in real time), a reset process with real identity proofing (not 'name + ID'), break-glass accounts that are monitored and alerted, and user education on the new flows. SMS (choice D) is the weakest factor (SIM-swap, interception) — better than nothing, worst of the options.

scenarios.title: The admin account everyone shares
scenarios.situation: The domain admin password is shared among 12 IT staff, written in a shared doc, and has not changed in 4 years. When something breaks, nobody knows who did what.
evidence: Field observation

Observed: The domain admin password is shared among 12 IT staff, written in a shared doc, and has not changed in 4 years. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
What 'done' looks like

Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Eliminate shared privileged credentials (2) Design just-in-time elevation Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct privileged access program?
choices: A. It works; changing it would slow down IT.

B. PAM: named admin accounts (no shared credentials), just-in-time elevation (request, approve, time-limited), session recording for sensitive systems, automated password rotation, and MFA on every privileged path — accountability and least privilege for the keys to the kingdom.
C. More people should have the password; bus factor.
D. Change the shared password monthly; sharing is fine if rotated.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the server broke at 3 AM. Which of the 12 did it? How would you ever know?
scenarios.why: Shared privileged credentials destroy the two things that matter most for powerful accounts: accountability (who did what — unknowable with 12 users on one password) and revocation (a departure means the password 'should' change, and never does). PAM fixes both structurally: each admin has a NAMED privileged account (actions attributable), elevation is just-in-time (request -> approve -> time-boxed access, then it expires), sessions on crown jewels are recorded, and the vault rotates passwords automatically. Monthly rotation of a shared password (choice D) keeps the accountability hole and adds calendar overhead. Standing privilege becomes zero-standing-privilege: no one HAS admin; they BORROW it, briefly, visibly.

scenarios.title: The bouncer at the door
scenarios.situation: A small office installs a firewall between their network and the internet. The owner asks what it actually does for them day to day.
scenarios.prompt: What is the firewall's job?
choices: It speeds up the internet connection
It encrypts every file on every computer
It blocks unsolicited inbound traffic and enforces rules about what may enter or leave — a bouncer with a guest list
It replaces the need for passwords
scenarios.why: A firewall is a policy enforcement point: it inspects traffic and allows or denies it based on rules — which addresses, ports, and directions are permitted. It does not encrypt your files or replace authentication; it controls the door so fewer attacks ever reach the inside.
scenarios.hint: Think about what a bouncer does — and does not do — at a club door.

scenarios.title: The customers on the company network
scenarios.situation: A cafe offers free Wi-Fi, but it runs on the same network as the point-of-sale system that processes card payments. A regular customer is studying networking.
scenarios.prompt: What is wrong with this setup, and what is the fix?
choices: The guest traffic shares a network with payment systems; isolate guest Wi-Fi on a separate network or VLAN away from business systems
Nothing — customers would never look at other devices
The Wi-Fi password should be removed to make it easier
The point-of-sale should be moved to the guest network
scenarios.why: Anyone on the same network can observe and potentially reach other devices on it. Guest traffic — untrusted by definition — must be segmented away from systems handling payments or business data. A separate guest network or VLAN is the standard, inexpensive fix.
scenarios.hint: Who else is on that network, and what could they reach?

scenarios.title: The laptop at the coffee shop
scenarios.situation: An employee needs to work from a coffee shop's public Wi-Fi and access files on the office server. Anyone nearby could be listening to the wireless traffic.
scenarios.prompt: How should the employee protect the connection?
choices: Turn the screen brightness down so nobody can read it
Only visit websites with nice designs
Public Wi-Fi is safe as long as you have antivirus
Use the company VPN — it encrypts traffic between the laptop and the office, shielding it from local eavesdroppers
scenarios.why: A virtual private network (VPN) builds an encrypted tunnel from the device to the trusted network, so anyone sniffing the coffee-shop Wi-Fi sees only scrambled traffic. It does not make the laptop itself secure — but it removes the network eavesdropper from the threat model.
scenarios.hint: What can the person at the next table see without protection?

scenarios.title: The router from 2012
scenarios.situation: An office access point still runs WEP security with the manufacturer's default admin password, and the network name broadcasts the company name.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct upgrade?
choices: Nothing — WEP was good enough in 2012 and nothing has changed
Move to WPA3 (or WPA2 at minimum), set a strong unique passphrase, and change the default admin credentials
Hide the network name — that alone stops attackers
Remove the password so guests connect easily
scenarios.why: WEP is broken — its encryption can be cracked in minutes — and default credentials are published in every manual online. Modern wireless security means WPA2 or WPA3 with a strong passphrase, unique admin credentials, and firmware updates. Hiding the network name (disabling SSID broadcast) is obscurity, not security.
scenarios.hint: Which of these settings would stop an attacker for more than a few minutes?

scenarios.title: The website that drowned
scenarios.situation: During the biggest sale of the year, an online store becomes unreachable. Traffic is a hundred times normal, coming from thousands of compromised devices worldwide — not real shoppers.
scenarios.prompt: What is happening, and what is the mitigation concept?
choices: A successful marketing campaign — buy a bigger server eventually
A worm — disconnect the store permanently
A distributed denial-of-service attack — absorb and filter the flood with a CDN, scrubbing service, or cloud scaling, and engage the ISP or provider
Normal holiday traffic — do nothing
scenarios.why: A DDoS attack overwhelms a target with traffic from a botnet, making the service unavailable to legitimate users — an attack on availability. You cannot block thousands of sources with a firewall rule; mitigation means absorbing the flood upstream (CDN, scrubbing centers, elastic scaling) and filtering attack traffic before it reaches you.
scenarios.hint: Is the goal to steal data, or to make the site unreachable?

scenarios.title: The free Wi-Fi that was not
scenarios.situation: At an airport, a traveler sees Free_Airport_WiFi with full signal and joins it. The hotspot is actually a laptop in an attacker's backpack, capturing every login the traveler types.
scenarios.prompt: How should travelers protect themselves from rogue hotspots?
choices: Always join the strongest free signal — signal strength proves legitimacy
Turn off the firewall to connect faster
Airports are safe, so no precautions are needed
Verify the official network name with staff, prefer a phone hotspot or VPN, and avoid sensitive logins on unknown networks
scenarios.why: An evil-twin attack mimics a legitimate hotspot to intercept traffic. Defenses: confirm the real network name with staff, use your phone's hotspot or a VPN so intercepted traffic is encrypted, and treat every unknown network as hostile. The attacker relies on convenience beating caution.
scenarios.hint: How would you know which hotspot is the real one?

scenarios.title: The open doors nobody uses
scenarios.situation: A scan of the office network finds an old printer with Telnet enabled — a service nobody uses or remembers configuring. The printer's firmware has not been updated in five years.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct action?
choices: Leave it — unused services cannot be attacked
Open more ports so the printer is easier to manage
Replace Telnet with a longer password
Disable the unneeded service and close the port — every open service is a potential entry point; shrink the attack surface
scenarios.why: Attack surface is the sum of reachable entry points: open ports, running services, enabled protocols. Unused services — especially ancient cleartext ones like Telnet — are pure risk with zero benefit. Hardening means disabling what you do not need, patching what you keep, and re-checking regularly.
scenarios.hint: What does the business gain from that open port? What could an attacker gain?

scenarios.title: The flat network that spread ransomware
scenarios.situation: Ransomware lands on one workstation and encrypts 400 servers in 20 minutes. The network is flat: every device can reach every other device on any port. No internal firewalls, no segments.
evidence: Field observation

Observed: Ransomware lands on one workstation and encrypts 400 servers in 20 minutes. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
What 'done' looks like
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Design network segmentation (2) Apply zero-trust principles Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What architectural principle would have contained it?
choices: A. Better antivirus on the workstation; the network is fine.

B. Segmentation and zero trust: divide the network into zones (user, server, OT, DMZ) with firewalls between, deny-by-default internal traffic, and 'never trust, always verify' per connection — lateral movement dies at the first segment boundary.
C. Faster incident response; architecture cannot stop ransomware.
D. Disconnect the internet; the LAN is trustworthy.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the ransomware moved workstation -> server 400 times. What would have stopped move #1?
scenarios.why: A flat network is a single failure domain: one compromised host can reach everything, so ransomware's lateral movement is unimpeded. Segmentation breaks the network into isolated zones with controlled chokepoints — the workstation VLAN cannot initiate SMB to the server VLAN, period. Zero trust extends the idea: no implicit trust by location (the LAN is not trustworthy — choice D is the old, dead model); every connection is authenticated, authorized, and encrypted regardless of where it originates. The 400 servers become unreachable from the workstation segment — the blast radius collapses from 'everything' to 'one zone.'

scenarios.title: The Wi-Fi password on the whiteboard
scenarios.situation: The office Wi-Fi uses one shared WPA2 password, written on the whiteboard in the lobby. Ex-employees, visitors, and the coffee shop next door all know it. Anyone on the network can sniff others' traffic.
evidence: Field observation

Observed: The office Wi-Fi uses one shared WPA2 password, written on the whiteboard in the lobby. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
What 'done' looks like
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Deploy enterprise wireless (2) Isolate guest traffic Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct wireless security design?
choices: A. Change the whiteboard password monthly; rotation fixes it.

B. WPA3 with enterprise authentication (802.1X + RADIUS): each user authenticates individually (unique credentials, no shared password), plus a separate isolated guest network — the whiteboard password model dies completely.
C. Hide the SSID; invisible networks are secure.
D. Stronger shared password, kept secret this time.
scenarios.hint: Hint: with a shared password, what stops an ex-employee from decrypting a current employee's traffic?
scenarios.why: A shared WPA2 passphrase (PSK) has two fatal properties: everyone with the password can decrypt everyone else's traffic (the pairwise keys derive from the shared secret), and the password cannot be revoked per-person — one departure means rotating it for all, which never happens. Enterprise mode (WPA2/WPA3-Enterprise with 802.1X against RADIUS/AD) gives each user unique credentials: traffic is individually encrypted, departures are one account disable, and access ties into identity lifecycle. WPA3 adds forward secrecy and stronger handshakes (SAE resists offline dictionary attacks). Hidden SSIDs (choice C) are trivially discoverable — obscurity, not security. A separate guest VLAN keeps visitors off the corporate network entirely.

scenarios.title: The alert nobody tuned
scenarios.situation: An IDS was deployed with default rules. It fires 5,000 alerts daily — 99% false positives. The team disabled notifications 'temporarily' two years ago. The breach it could have caught went unnoticed.
evidence: Field observation
Observed: An IDS was deployed with default rules. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
What 'done' looks like
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Tune IDS rules (2) Decide IDS vs IPS placement Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct IDS/IPS program?
choices: A. IDS is useless; the false positives prove it.

B. Tune to the environment (disable irrelevant rules, baseline normal, write custom rules for your threats), tier the deployment (IDS detect + IPS prevent on well-understood signatures), and measure precision — an IDS is a detection instrument that must be calibrated, not a plug-and-play oracle.
C. Enable IPS blocking on all default rules; blocking fixes false positives.
D. More sensors; coverage was the problem.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the IDS saw the breach traffic. Why did no human ever look at the alert?
scenarios.why: Default rule sets fire on everything because they know nothing about your environment: the SQL-injection rule alerts on your developers' legitimate admin tool, the Tor rule fires on the research team. Tuning is the job: disable rules for services you do not run, baseline what normal looks like, write rules for YOUR threats (the custom app's attack surface), and track precision per rule. IPS blocking on untuned rules (choice C) turns false positives into self-inflicted outages — block only on high-precision signatures. Placement matters too: IDS sees (detect), IPS acts (prevent) — and both need the decrypted/visible traffic (TLS inspection or endpoint context) to see modern attacks.

scenarios.title: The break-in with no witnesses
scenarios.situation: A server is compromised, but the company kept almost no logs. Nobody can say when the attacker got in, what they touched, or whether they are still inside.
scenarios.prompt: What is the lesson for security operations?
choices: Logs are optional — the antivirus will write the incident report
Centralized logging enables detection and investigation: without logs, you cannot see the attack or scope the damage
Delete logs regularly so attackers cannot read them
Only large companies need logging
scenarios.why: Logs are the witnesses of the digital world: they record who did what and when. Centralized collection (often in a SIEM) lets analysts detect patterns and reconstruct incidents. No logs means no timeline, no scope, and no confident recovery — you are guessing in the dark.
scenarios.hint: What would a detective say about a crime scene with no witnesses and no cameras?

scenarios.title: The update everyone postponed
scenarios.situation: Attackers breach a company through a vulnerability the vendor patched eight months ago. The patch was marked low priority and never scheduled.
scenarios.prompt: What process failed, and what does good look like?
choices: Patch management — inventory systems, test patches, and deploy them on a schedule; known vulnerabilities are the attacker's favorite door
Antivirus — it should have stopped a patched vulnerability
Hiring — the team needed more people to ignore updates
Nothing failed — patching is optional
scenarios.why: Most breaches exploit known vulnerabilities with available patches — attackers automate scanning for unpatched systems within hours of disclosure. Patch management is the disciplined cycle: know what you have, test the fix, deploy it promptly, and verify. Postponed patches are open invitations.
scenarios.hint: Did the attackers discover something new, or use something everyone knew about?

scenarios.title: The admin admin camera
scenarios.situation: An attacker logs into the office security cameras using the default username and password printed in the manufacturer's manual, then watches the building for weeks.
scenarios.prompt: What is the fix, and what broader practice does it belong to?
choices: Change all default credentials as part of system hardening — defaults are public knowledge, not secrets
Unplug the cameras — they are the problem
The manual should be kept secret instead
Longer camera cables
scenarios.why: Default credentials are published in manuals and online lists — attackers try them first. Hardening a system means changing defaults, disabling unneeded services, and applying secure baselines before it touches the network. Every device with admin/admin still set is an open door with a welcome mat.
scenarios.hint: Where else could an attacker find that default password?

scenarios.title: The email that looked like the boss
scenarios.situation: An employee receives an urgent email that appears to be from the CEO, asking them to buy gift cards for client gifts and send the codes immediately.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct action?
choices: Do not reply or buy anything; report it to IT or security through the phishing report button — this is a classic gift-card scam
Buy the gift cards — the CEO's name is on the email
Reply asking which store the CEO prefers
Forward it to friends so they can get gift cards too
scenarios.why: No executive requests gift cards by email — urgency plus an unusual request is the signature of this scam. The right move is to stop, not engage, and report it so security can warn others and block the sender. Reporting turns one near-miss into protection for the whole company.
scenarios.hint: Has your CEO ever asked anyone to buy gift cards by email?

scenarios.title: The spreadsheet marked confidential
scenarios.situation: The company labels data as Public, Internal, or Confidential. A new employee wonders why a customer list marked Confidential cannot be emailed to a personal account for weekend work.
scenarios.prompt: Why does classification matter?
choices: Labels are decoration — data is data
Only the CEO may see Confidential data
Public data needs the strongest protection
Classification drives handling rules: Confidential data gets encryption, sharing limits, and retention rules matched to its sensitivity
scenarios.why: Data classification assigns each type of information a sensitivity level, and each level carries handling rules: how it is stored, shared, encrypted, and eventually destroyed. Without labels, everything is treated the same — which means the crown jewels get the same protection as the lunch menu.
scenarios.hint: Should the lunch menu and the customer database be protected identically?

scenarios.title: The laptop left on the train
scenarios.situation: An employee leaves a laptop on a train. It holds customer records — but the entire disk was encrypted, and the loss is reported within the hour so the password can be rotated and the device remotely locked.
scenarios.prompt: Why is this incident a recovery story instead of a data breach?
choices: The train company is trustworthy
Full-disk encryption keeps the data unreadable without the key — a lost encrypted device is a hardware loss, not a data exposure
Customer records are not sensitive
Encryption only matters for email
scenarios.why: Encryption at rest protects data on lost or stolen devices: without the key, the disk is scrambled noise to whoever finds it. Paired with quick reporting, remote lock, and credential rotation, the incident stays a lost laptop instead of becoming a breach notification. Encrypt mobile devices by default — loss is a matter of when.
scenarios.hint: What can the finder actually read on that disk?

scenarios.title: The one screen that watches everything
scenarios.situation: A small security team is drowning in separate logs from firewalls, servers, and laptops. They deploy a SIEM that pulls the logs into one place and raises alerts on suspicious patterns.
scenarios.prompt: What value does the SIEM add for a junior analyst?
choices: Centralized collection plus correlation and alerting: one place to search, and patterns across sources surface automatically instead of checking devices one by one
It replaces analysts entirely — the SIEM makes all decisions
It makes the logs prettier
It deletes old logs to save disk space
scenarios.why: A SIEM (security information and event management) centralizes logs so analysts can search everything at once, and its correlation rules connect events across sources into meaningful alerts. It does not replace judgment — it focuses it: fewer places to look, higher-quality leads to investigate.
scenarios.hint: What is harder: checking fifty devices, or searching one screen?

scenarios.title: The patch that broke payroll
scenarios.situation: A critical security patch is rushed to all servers Friday night — and breaks payroll processing. Monday's payroll is late for 5,000 employees. Next month, the team delays patches 'to be safe' — and gets breached through the unpatched flaw.
evidence: Field observation

Observed: A critical security patch is rushed to all servers Friday night — and breaks payroll processing. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
What 'done' looks like
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Run risk-based patching (2) Deploy in rings with rollback Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct patch management lifecycle?
choices: A. Patch everything immediately; breakage is acceptable collateral.

B. Risk-based patching with testing: inventory assets, prioritize by severity x exposure, test critical patches in a staging/canary group, deploy in rings (canary -> broad), with rollback plans — speed for the critical-exposed, safety for the fragile, and never 'delay indefinitely.'
C. Delay all patches a month; stability first.
D. Only patch when breached; patching is the risk.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the rushed patch and the delayed patch both failed. What process succeeds at both speed AND safety?
scenarios.why: Both failures in the scenario are process failures: the rushed patch skipped testing (breakage), the delayed patch skipped urgency (breach). The lifecycle balances them: asset inventory (what needs patching), prioritization (internet-facing critical CVE = hours; internal low = next window), testing (staging or canary group catches the payroll break), ring deployment (canary -> 10% -> all, with health checks between), and rollback readiness. Emergency patches for actively exploited criticals still go fast — but through the canary, not around it. 'Delay to be safe' (choice C) is how the breach happened; the patch was the fix, the process was the problem.

scenarios.title: The phishing test with a 40% click rate
scenarios.situation: The annual security training is a 45-minute video everyone plays at 2x while doing email. The simulated phishing test: 40% click rate. Leadership asks why training 'does not work.'
evidence: Field observation

Observed: The annual security training is a 45-minute video everyone plays at 2x while doing email. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
What 'done' looks like

Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Build effective awareness programs (2) Use phishing simulation correctly Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What makes awareness training actually change behavior?
choices: A. Longer videos; 45 minutes was not enough.

B. Short, frequent, role-relevant training plus simulated phishing with immediate teachable moments (the click lands on a 60-second lesson, not a shaming email), measured by behavior change (click-rate trend, reporting rate) — and a reporting culture where the fast reporter is praised.
C. Punish clickers; fear teaches.
D. Training is hopeless; rely on technical controls only.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the clicker just demonstrated exactly when they are most teachable. What happens in the 60 seconds after the click?
scenarios.why: Annual videos fail for known reasons: forgetting curve (one dose decays in weeks), irrelevance (finance needs BEC training, developers need secure-coding, not the same video), and no practice (watching is not doing). What works: micro-training (5-10 minutes, monthly), role-based content, simulated phishing as practice (the click becomes a 60-second lesson AT the moment of failure — the teachable instant), and metrics that matter (click rate trending down, REPORTING rate trending up — reporters are the human sensors). Punishment (choice C) suppresses reporting — the opposite of what you want. Technical controls are essential AND insufficient: the phish that bypasses the filter meets the human.

scenarios.title: The laptop fleet with local admin everywhere
scenarios.situation: Every user is a local admin on their laptop 'so IT gets fewer tickets.' Malware runs with admin rights, disables the EDR, and spreads. The help-desk ticket savings cost a breach.
evidence: Field observation

Observed: Every user is a local admin on their laptop 'so IT gets fewer tickets.' Malware runs with admin rights, disables the EDR, and spreads. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
What 'done' looks like
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Harden endpoints (2) Remove standing local admin Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct endpoint hardening posture?
choices: A. Keep local admin; user productivity outweighs the risk.

B. Least privilege on endpoints: standard users by default, elevation via approved workflow (JIT admin or allowlisted installers), EDR on every endpoint with tamper protection, disk encryption, and a hardened baseline image — the ticket cost is real and far cheaper than the breach.
C. Remove all software installation; users get a fixed image forever.
D. EDR alone is enough; admin rights do not matter with good EDR.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the malware disabled the EDR. What permission did that require?
scenarios.why: Local admin for everyone trades a chronic, catastrophic risk for ticket convenience: malware inherits admin (disables defenses, persists, spreads), and every phishing click becomes a system compromise. The posture: users run standard (malware inherits standard), legitimate elevation goes through a workflow (self-service allowlisted apps, JIT elevation with approval for the rest), EDR with tamper protection on everything (so admin-malware cannot blind it), encrypted disks, and baseline images. The ticket concern is legitimate — answer it with self-service and fast elevation, not with standing admin. EDR-alone (choice D) fails precisely because admin malware kills the EDR first.

scenarios.title: The Security Principles Mystery
scenarios.situation: Users report that Security Principles is not working correctly. The obvious checks pass — the components are online, basic connectivity works. You need to think in systems, not symptoms.
scenarios.prompt: Using the systems anatomy method (whole → cut open → step through → pull apart), how would you systematically trace a failure in Security Principles?
choices: Walk the full journey: start from the trigger, verify each handoff in sequence, check dependencies at every step, and isolate where the flow breaks — then examine that specific layer
Restart all components — Security Principles issues are always fixed by restarting
Check the most common cause from memory and apply that fix immediately
Escalate to senior support — Security Principles is too complex to troubleshoot systematically
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Systems thinking means tracing the living flow: (1) Whole: what is Security Principles supposed to do end-to-end? (2) Cut open: what are the layers/stages? (3) Step through: verify each handoff — where does the expected output diverge from actual? (4) Pull apart: isolate the broken layer and examine it in detail. This method works for any Security Principles failure in Isc2 Cc.
scenarios.hint: Don't jump to the fix. First map the journey, then find where it breaks.
objectives: Apply systems anatomy to Security Principles
evidence: System Status

User Report
Functionality is broken despite green status indicators. The failure is in the flow, not the components.

domains.name: Risk Management
domains.description: Identifying assets, analyzing risk qualitatively and quantitatively, and treating risk — the decision discipline behind every control.

scenarios.title: The server room nobody inventoried
scenarios.situation: A company wants a risk assessment but has no inventory: nobody knows how many servers exist, where customer data lives, or which systems are critical. The consultant is asked to 'assess the risk' anyway.
objectives: Structure a risk assessment per asset
evidence: Field observation

Observed: A company wants a risk assessment but has no inventory: nobody knows how many servers exist, where customer data lives, or which systems are critical. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
What 'done' looks like

Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Build an asset inventory (2) Structure a risk assessment per asset Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct first step?
choices: A. Assess anyway — a risk assessment is about threats, not inventories.
B. Build the asset inventory first (systems, data, owners, criticality): you cannot assess risk to assets you cannot name. Then identify threats and vulnerabilities per asset.
C. Start by buying security tools; the assessment can follow.
D. Interview executives about their worries; perception is the inventory.
scenarios.hint: Hint: risk to WHAT? Name the thing first.
scenarios.why: Risk is always risk TO something: an asset with value, facing a threat, through a vulnerability. Without an inventory, 'risk assessment' produces generic fears untethered from the business — you cannot prioritize protecting the customer database if you do not know it exists. The standard order is: inventory assets and classify data, identify threats to each, identify vulnerabilities, then analyze likelihood and impact. Executive worries (choice D) inform priorities but are not a substitute for knowing what you own.

scenarios.title: The $2M firewall question
scenarios.situation: Leadership asks whether a $2M security investment is justified. The risk team has two analyses: a heat map (High/Medium/Low) and a quantitative model showing $3.1M annualized loss expectancy without the control vs $900K with it.
evidence: Field observation

Observed: Leadership asks whether a $2M security investment is justified. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
What 'done' looks like

Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Compute SLE, ARO, and ALE (2) Choose qualitative vs quantitative analysis Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: Which analysis answers the budget question, and why?
choices: A. The heat map — executives understand colors better than numbers.
B. The quantitative analysis: ALE = SLE x ARO turns risk into dollars, so the $2M cost can be compared against the $2.2M expected savings. Heat maps prioritize; only quantification justifies spend.
C. Neither — security spending is never justifiable with math.
D. Whichever is shorter; executives do not read long analyses.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the question is 'is $2M justified?' — what unit must the answer be in?
scenarios.why: Qualitative analysis (High/Medium/Low heat maps) is fast and good for prioritizing a list of risks relative to each other. But a budget decision is a comparison of dollars: quantitative analysis computes Single Loss Expectancy (SLE = asset value x exposure factor), Annualized Rate of Occurrence (ARO), and Annualized Loss Expectancy (ALE = SLE x ARO). Here ALE drops from $3.1M to $900K — a $2.2M expected saving against a $2M cost, a positive return. The heat map cannot do this math; it can only say the risk is 'High' before and 'Medium' after, which justifies nothing numerically.

scenarios.title: The legacy system that cannot be patched
scenarios.situation: A 15-year-old billing system cannot be patched (vendor dead, source lost) but cannot be retired for two years. It processes $50M annually and is network-reachable. The risk is rated High.
evidence: Field observation

Observed: A 15-year-old billing system cannot be patched (vendor dead, source lost) but cannot be retired for two years. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
What 'done' looks like

Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Apply the four risk treatments (2) Document residual risk acceptance Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct risk treatment?
choices: A. Accept the risk — nothing can be done, so formalize doing nothing.

B. Mitigate with compensating controls: isolate it on a segmented network, restrict access to jump hosts with MFA, monitor it heavily, and back it up — reduce likelihood and impact while the replacement is built. Document the residual risk and get formal acceptance of THAT.
C. Transfer the risk by buying cyber insurance and changing nothing technically.
D. Avoid the risk by unplugging it immediately, whatever the business cost.
scenarios.hint: Hint: which option both protects the $50M process AND shrinks the risk while the replacement is built?
scenarios.why: The four treatments: avoid (stop the activity), transfer (insurance/outsourcing — transfers financial impact, not the breach itself), mitigate (controls that reduce likelihood/impact), accept (formal, informed, time-boxed). Unplugging (choice D) avoids the risk by killing the business process — avoidance must be proportionate. Insurance (choice C) transfers some financial loss but not the operational outage, the customer harm, or the regulatory fallout — and insurers now require controls anyway. Pure acceptance (choice A) of a High, unmitigated risk is negligence with paperwork. Mitigation via compensating controls is the professional answer: segmentation, access control, monitoring, and backups shrink the risk while the real fix (replacement) proceeds — and the documented residual risk gets genuine informed acceptance.

scenarios.title: The vendor with the master key
scenarios.situation: A payroll vendor has VPN access into the company network and stores employee SSNs. The vendor was breached last year. Your company has never assessed the vendor's security — the contract has no security requirements.
evidence: Field observation

Observed: A payroll vendor has VPN access into the company network and stores employee SSNs. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
What 'done' looks like

Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Tier and assess vendors (2) Write security requirements into contracts Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct third-party risk program?
choices: A. Nothing — the vendor's security is the vendor's problem.

B. Tier vendors by data/system access, assess the critical ones (questionnaires, evidence, or audits), put security requirements in contracts (breach notification, right to audit, data handling), and limit their access to least privilege — your data in their hands is still your risk.
C. Terminate all vendors; in-house everything.
D. Ask the vendor 'are you secure?' once a year and file the yes.

A yearly 'are you secure?' (choice D) is theater; in-housing everything (choice C) is fantasy.

scenarios.title: The risk everyone forgot
scenarios.situation: Two years ago a risk assessment flagged 'single internet provider' as High. Nothing was done, nobody owned it, and last week's 8-hour ISP outage cost $400K. The risk was real, documented, and then forgotten.
evidence: Field observation

Observed: Two years ago a risk assessment flagged 'single internet provider' as High. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
What 'done' looks like

Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Maintain a risk register (2) Assign ownership and review cadence Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What practice prevents documented risks from dying in a spreadsheet?
choices: A. Longer risk reports; the problem was the report was too short to be taken seriously.

B. A living risk register: each risk has an owner, a treatment plan, a review date, and residual-risk status — reviewed on a cadence by people with authority. Documentation without ownership and review is archiving, not management.
C. Delete old risks; if it mattered it would have been fixed.
D. Blame the ISP; the risk was theirs.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the risk was documented AND forgotten. What turns a document into management?
scenarios.why: A risk register is a management tool, not a document: the columns that matter are owner (a named human), treatment (what is being done), residual rating (after treatment), and review date (when we look again). The ISP outage was foreseeable and foreseen — the failure was governance: no owner, no treatment, no review, so the risk sat until it materialized. Cadence reviews (monthly/quarterly, with leadership for High risks) force the re-decision: treat, accept formally, or escalate. Longer reports (choice A) add words, not accountability.

scenarios.title: The signature before go-live
scenarios.situation: A new customer portal launches Friday. The risk assessment found two Medium residual risks (no WAF yet, logs not yet centralized). Engineering wants to launch; security wants to block. Leadership must decide.
evidence: Field observation
Observed: A new customer portal launches Friday. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
What 'done' looks like
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Govern residual risk acceptance Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct governance?
choices: A. Block the launch — no residual risk is acceptable before go-live.

B. Present the residual risks plainly (likelihood, impact, planned mitigations with dates), let the accountable executive formally accept or defer — the decision, the rationale, and the mitigation deadlines are documented. Security advises; the business decides with eyes open.
C. Launch silently and fix later; asking creates liability.
D. Let engineering and security vote; majority wins.
scenarios.hint: Hint: whose job is it to decide how much risk the business takes — security's, or the business's?
scenarios.why: Residual risk acceptance is a business decision, not a security veto: security's job is to make the risk legible (what could happen, how likely, what it costs, what the mitigations are and when they land); the accountable executive's job is to accept or defer formally. Blocking all residual risk (choice A) would block every launch — all systems have residual risk. Silent launching (choice C) converts a manageable risk into a governance failure and personal liability. The documented acceptance (with mitigation deadlines) is what auditors and boards expect: risk managed transparently, not risk hidden or risk absolutism.
