scenarios.title: The clean scan before the breach
scenarios.situation: Quarterly vulnerability scans are clean, yet an attacker breached the company through a chained attack: a low-severity info disclosure plus a misconfigured service the scanner did not test. Leadership asks what the scans missed.
evidence: Field observation

Observed: Quarterly vulnerability scans are clean, yet an attacker breached the company through a chained attack: a low-severity info disclosure plus a misconfigured service the scanner did not test. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
What 'done' looks like

Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Distinguish scans from pentests (2) Design an assessment cadence Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct explanation of assessment types?
choices: A. Scans are useless; only penetration tests matter.

B. Vulnerability scans check known issues against signatures (broad, shallow, automated); penetration tests have humans chaining weaknesses toward an objective (narrow, deep, creative). The scan was clean because chaining and logic flaws are outside its model — the program needs both, plus configuration review.
C. The scanner was misconfigured; a better scanner would have found the chain.
D. Penetration tests are just expensive scans; run scans more often instead.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the attacker combined two 'lows' into a breach. Which assessment type thinks in combinations?
scenarios.why: Scans and pentests answer different questions: a scanner asks 'which known vulnerabilities exist on these hosts?' (CVE signatures, fast, broad); a pentester asks 'can an attacker reach the objective?' (chaining lows into highs, business logic, misconfigurations — slow, deep, human). The chained attack lived in the gap between the models: each weakness was low alone, devastating combined — exactly what human testers do and scanners do not. A 'better scanner' (choice C) still does not chain; more scans (choice D) repeat the same model. The mature program runs both on cadence, plus configuration/baseline reviews for the misconfiguration class.

scenarios.title: The auditor's first question
scenarios.situation: An external auditor arrives for the annual security audit and asks: 'Show me your access-review records for the past year.' The company did the reviews verbally — no records exist.
evidence: Field observation

Observed: An external auditor arrives for the annual security audit and asks: 'Show me your access-review records for the past year.' The company did the reviews verbally — no records exist. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
What 'done' looks like

Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Explain what auditors verify (2) Design evidence-generating controls Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What does this teach about audits?
choices: A. Auditors are unreasonable; verbal reviews should count.

B. Audits test evidence, not activity: a control without evidence (records, logs, tickets) fails the audit regardless of what actually happened. Build evidence generation into the control (review tickets, approval logs, attestations).
C. The answer is to do fewer reviews so there is less to evidence.
D. Audits only matter for regulated industries; others can ignore them.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the auditor cannot observe the past. What CAN they observe?
scenarios.why: An audit is an independent verification that controls operate as claimed — and verification runs on evidence. 'We did it but did not record it' is indistinguishable from 'we did not do it,' so the control fails. The fix is designing controls that produce evidence by construction: access reviews as tickets with approver + timestamp, changes as approved change records, training as completion logs. Internal audits (self-checks), external audits (independent), and third-party audits (of vendors) all share this property. Fewer reviews (choice C) reduces both security and evidence — the wrong direction twice.

scenarios.title: The servers that drifted
scenarios.situation: All servers were hardened at build, but three years later a review finds Telnet enabled on some, default SNMP strings on others, and inconsistent patch levels. Nothing enforced the baseline after day one.
evidence: Field observation

Observed: All servers were hardened at build, but three years later a review finds Telnet enabled on some, default SNMP strings on others, and inconsistent patch levels. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
What 'done' looks like
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Define hardening baselines (2) Build the baseline lifecycle Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What practice keeps systems hardened over time?
choices: A. Harden once at build; drift is inevitable and harmless.

B. Define a written baseline (hardening standard), deploy it via automation (images, configuration management), and continuously verify compliance (config scanning) — hardening is a maintained state, not a one-time event.
C. Harden harder initially; a sufficiently strict build never drifts.
D. Let each admin harden to taste; diversity is resilience.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the servers were fine on day one. What maintains 'fine' on day one thousand?
scenarios.why: Configuration drift is entropy: manual changes, emergency fixes, and staff turnover move systems off baseline within months. The defense is a loop: a written standard (what 'hardened' means — CIS Benchmarks are the industry reference), automated deployment (golden images, Ansible/Puppet/Chef — the baseline is code), and continuous verification (configuration scanners that flag drift for remediation). One-time hardening (choices A/C) decays; admin taste (choice D) is not a standard — it is fifteen standards, none verifiable.

scenarios.title: The critical finding from 2023
scenarios.situation: A 2023 pentest found a critical SQL injection. The report was emailed, discussed once, and filed. A 2025 retest finds the same injection — now with customer data behind it. The finding was never tracked.
evidence: Field observation
Observed: A 2023 pentest found a critical SQL injection. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
What 'done' looks like
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Run a finding lifecycle (2) Verify fixes independently Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What system ensures findings become fixes?
choices: A. Better reports; the 2023 report was not persuasive enough.

B. A single remediation backlog: every finding becomes a ticket with severity, owner, SLA (critical: days, high: weeks), and verification of the fix (retest, not self-attestation). Reports feed the backlog; the backlog is reviewed until empty.
C. More frequent pentests; the retest would have caught it sooner.
D. Accept that some findings never get fixed.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the finding was KNOWN for two years. What was missing between 'known' and 'fixed'?
scenarios.why: Findings die in reports; they live in backlogs. The system is: ingest every finding (scans, pentests, audits) into ONE tracker, assign severity by a consistent rubric, assign an owner, set an SLA clock (critical 7-15 days, high 30, medium 90 — tuned to the org), and verify closure by retest — the fixer does not grade their own fix. Leadership reviews aging findings; anything past SLA escalates. The 2023 injection survived because no ticket, no owner, no clock, and no verification existed — the report was a message in a bottle. More pentests (choice C) would have produced more ignored reports.

scenarios.title: The backup that was never restored
scenarios.situation: Backups ran nightly for years — green checkmarks every morning. During a ransomware incident, the restore fails: the backup job backed up the wrong directory for 18 months. Nobody ever tested a restore.
evidence: Field observation

Observed: Backups ran nightly for years — green checkmarks every morning. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
What 'done' looks like

Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Test controls against their objectives (2) Schedule and evidence control tests Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What does this teach about controls?
choices: A. Backups are unreliable; switch to a different backup product.

B. A control is only proven by testing its objective: backups exist to RESTORE, so the test is a restore (regular test restores, documented). Monitoring the job's success monitored the wrong thing — activity, not outcome.
C. Run backups twice daily; more backups would have helped.
D. The backup admin should be fired; the product was fine.
scenarios.hint: Hint: what is a backup FOR? Now, what did the green checkmark actually prove?
scenarios.why: Every control has an objective, and the test must exercise the objective: a backup's objective is successful restoration, so the control test is a periodic test restore (to an isolated location, documented, with timing). The green checkmarks tested 'did the job run' — activity — while the objective silently failed for 18 months. This generalizes: test firewalls by attempting blocked traffic, test MFA by attempting bypass, test incident response with tabletops. More backups (choice C) would have doubled the wrong-directory copies; the product (choice A) was never the problem.

scenarios.title: The report nobody read
scenarios.situation: A 60-page technical pentest report went to the board. Nobody read it; the critical findings were not funded. The board needed a decision document, not a vulnerability dump.
evidence: Field observation
Observed: A 60-page technical pentest report went to the board. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
What 'done' looks like
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Communicate risk to executives Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: How should findings be communicated upward?
choices: A. Send the full technical report; the board should learn the details.

B. Executive summary: business risk per finding (what breaks, what it costs, likelihood), prioritized actions with costs and owners, and the 'so what' in business language — one page per critical, appendix for technicians. Fundability is the metric.
C. Only report good news; bad news gets ignored anyway.
D. Have the pentesters present live; charisma fixes communication.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the board funds business cases. What does a CVE number mean to a CFO?
scenarios.why: Executives fund what they understand: translate each critical finding into business risk (system affected, business impact in dollars/downtime, likelihood) and pair it with a specific ask (action, cost, owner, timeline). The technical report becomes the appendix — evidence for the engineers, not the decision document. One page per critical, plain language, no CVE numbers in the summary: 'Customer database extractable via the customer portal; estimated breach cost $2-5M; fix: input validation + WAF, $80K, 30 days, owner: app team.' That paragraph gets funded; 60 pages do not.

domains.name: Applied Cryptography
domains.description: Encryption, hashing, PKI, TLS, and key management — what cryptography actually guarantees, and where it breaks in practice.

scenarios.title: The key exchange problem
scenarios.situation: Two branch offices need encrypted file transfers. Symmetric encryption (AES) is fast, but securely sharing the secret key between offices is unsolved — emailing the key defeats the purpose.
evidence: Field observation
Observed: Two branch offices need encrypted file transfers. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
What 'done' looks like

Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Explain hybrid encryption (2) Choose symmetric vs asymmetric correctly Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct cryptographic design?
choices: A. Email the AES key; the transfer itself is encrypted, which is what matters.

B. Hybrid encryption: use asymmetric crypto (RSA/ECC) to securely exchange a per-session symmetric key, then AES for the bulk data — asymmetric solves key distribution, symmetric provides speed. (This is what TLS does.)
C. Use asymmetric encryption for the entire file; public-key crypto for bulk data is fine.
D. Skip encryption; the offices trust each other.
scenarios.hint: Hint: what is the ONE thing symmetric encryption cannot do for you — and what can?
scenarios.why: Symmetric crypto's hard problem is key distribution: the key must be shared without being intercepted, which is the very problem encryption was meant to solve. Asymmetric crypto splits the key into public (shareable) and private (secret): anyone can encrypt to the public key, only the private-key holder decrypts — key distribution becomes safe. But asymmetric is ~1000x slower, so real systems are hybrid: asymmetric negotiates a session key, symmetric (AES) encrypts the bulk. Emailing the key (choice A) hands the adversary the lock and the key together; pure-asymmetric bulk (choice C) is impractically slow.

scenarios.title: The downloaded installer
scenarios.situation: You download a critical installer. The vendor publishes a SHA-256 hash. Your computed hash matches — or does not. A colleague says 'hashing is encryption, so the file is now encrypted.'
evidence: Field observation
Observed: You download a critical installer. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
What 'done' looks like
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Verify file integrity (2) Explain what hashes guarantee Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What do hashes actually guarantee, and what is the correct verification?
choices: A. The colleague is right: hashing encrypts, so the download is now secure.

B. Hashes provide integrity, not secrecy: a matching SHA-256 (from a trusted channel) proves the file was not altered or corrupted in transit. It does not encrypt anything, and the hash itself must come from the vendor's authentic site — a hash on the same compromised page proves nothing.
C. Hashes are obsolete; skip verification.
D. Any matching hash (even MD5) is fine for security.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the hash tells you the file MATCHES. Matches what — and where did 'what' come from?
scenarios.why: A cryptographic hash is a one-way fingerprint: easy to compute, infeasible to reverse or to find two files with the same digest (for SHA-256). Matching digests prove the bytes you got are the bytes the vendor published — integrity against corruption and tampering. Hashing is not encryption (choice A is flatly wrong): the file is unchanged and readable; only its fingerprint was compared. Two caveats: the expected hash must arrive via a trusted channel (an attacker who replaces the file replaces the published hash too — verify from the vendor's HTTPS site or signed release notes), and MD5/SHA-1 are broken for security (collisions are practical) — use SHA-256 or better.

scenarios.title: The browser warning
scenarios.situation: Users report a browser warning: 'Your connection is not private — certificate expired' on the company portal. IT's proposed fix is telling users to click through the warning.
evidence: Field observation

Observed: Users report a browser warning: 'Your connection is not private — certificate expired' on the company portal. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
What 'done' looks like

Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Explain the certificate chain (2) Respond to certificate warnings correctly Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is actually wrong, and what is the correct fix?
choices: A. Clicking through is fine; the warning is just bureaucracy.

B. The certificate (the site's authenticated public key, signed by a trusted CA) expired — renew it via the CA (ideally automated with ACME/Let's Encrypt-style renewal), and NEVER train users to click through warnings: that habit is exactly what phishing exploits.
C. Buy a more expensive certificate; price determines trust.
D. Disable HTTPS; the warnings go away.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the warning exists to stop users at the exact moment authentication fails. What does clicking through teach them?
scenarios.why: A TLS certificate binds the site's public key to its identity, signed by a Certificate Authority the browser trusts — the padlock is authentication, not just encryption. Expiry breaks the chain: the browser cannot verify the binding is current, so it warns. The fix is renewal (automated — 90-day certs with ACME renewal eliminate this class of outage), not click-through training: users who learn to bypass warnings will bypass the warning on the phishing clone too. Certificate price (choice C) does not affect trust — domain-validated certs from free CAs are cryptographically identical for this purpose.

scenarios.title: The padlock on the phishing site
scenarios.situation: A phishing email links to a site with a valid padlock (https://secure-login-portal.example). A user argues 'it has the padlock, so it must be the real login page.' Credentials are entered.
evidence: Field observation

Observed: A phishing email links to a site with a valid padlock (https://secure-login-portal.example). Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
What 'done' looks like

Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Explain TLS guarantees precisely (2) Teach domain verification Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What does the padlock actually prove — and not prove?
choices: A. The padlock proves the site is legitimate and safe.

B. The padlock proves the CONNECTION is encrypted to whoever holds that domain's certificate — it says nothing about whether the domain itself is trustworthy. Attackers get free valid certificates for lookalike domains routinely. Verify the DOMAIN NAME, not the padlock.
C. The padlock is meaningless; ignore it entirely.
D. Only expensive certificates are trustworthy; free ones indicate phishing.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the padlock authenticates the domain. Who chose the domain?
scenarios.why: TLS provides two things: encryption (no eavesdropping) and authentication (you are talking to the holder of the certificate for THIS domain). It does NOT provide reputation: a certificate for 'secure-login-portal.example' is validly issued to the attacker who registered that lookalike domain — the padlock is working correctly, authenticating the wrong party. Domain-validated certificates (including free ones) prove control of the domain, not legitimacy of the business — that is by design. The defense is reading the actual domain name (and using password managers, which refuse to fill on wrong domains, plus MFA).

scenarios.title: The key in the source code
scenarios.situation: An encryption key is hardcoded in the application source, committed to git, and copied to every developer laptop. The data is 'encrypted' — and the key is everywhere.
evidence: Field observation

Observed: An encryption key is hardcoded in the application source, committed to git, and copied to every developer laptop. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
What 'done' looks like

Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Explain key management lifecycle (2) Remediate exposed secrets Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: Why is this broken, and what is the correct key management?
choices: A. It is fine; the repository is private.

B. The encryption is theater: anyone with repo access (or any laptop, or any git history) has the key. Keys belong in a KMS/HSM or secrets manager, injected at runtime, with rotation, access audit, and separation — cryptography's security lives in key management, not the algorithm.
C. Obfuscate the key in the code; obfuscation is sufficient.
D. Use a longer hardcoded key; length compensates for exposure.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the algorithm is AES-256, unbreakable. So where is the actual vulnerability?
scenarios.why: Encryption's security reduces entirely to key secrecy: AES-256 with a public key is plaintext with extra steps. A hardcoded key is exposed to every repo reader, every laptop, every backup, and forever in git history (deleting it later does not purge history). 'Private repo' (choice A) is not access control for secrets — developers join, leave, and get phished. Correct practice: keys generated in and never leaving a KMS/HSM, referenced by alias; applications get data keys or decrypt via API; rotation scheduled; access logged; developers never see production keys. Longer keys (choice D) and obfuscation (choice C) do not fix distribution — the key is still everywhere.

scenarios.title: The laptop left on the train — encrypted?
scenarios.situation: An executive's laptop is stolen. It had full disk encryption (FDE) enabled — but the laptop was asleep (not powered off), and the password was on a sticky note in the bag.
evidence: Field observation
Observed: An executive's laptop is stolen. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
What 'done' looks like
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Explain FDE guarantees and limits Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What does FDE actually protect against, and what failed here?
choices: A. FDE failed; encryption does not work against theft.

B. FDE protects data at rest against offline attacks (disk removed, powered-off device) — it worked as designed. What failed was operational: sleep keeps keys in memory (cold-boot/DMA attacks possible), and the sticky-note password bypassed the authentication the encryption depends on.
C. The laptop should not have been encrypted; encryption attracts thieves.
D. FDE protects against everything, so the data is safe regardless.
scenarios.hint: Hint: FDE encrypts the disk. When is the disk's content accessible without the password?
scenarios.why: FDE's guarantee is narrow and precise: without the key (derived from your password/TPM), the disk's bits are unreadable to anyone who takes the DRIVE. It does not protect a running/sleeping system — keys live in RAM, and the OS will happily decrypt for anyone who wakes it. The sticky note is the classic failure: encryption's strength is irrelevant when the key is in the bag. Correct posture: FDE everywhere (BitLocker/FileVault/LUKS), powered OFF (not sleep) when traveling, strong passwords, and remote-wipe MDM — each control covers what FDE does not.

domains.name: SOC Fundamentals
domains.description: SIEM, alert triage, playbooks, threat intelligence, and escalation — how security operations centers turn signal into response.

scenarios.title: The log nobody read
scenarios.situation: After a breach, investigators find the attacker's logins in the VPN logs — collected for two years, never reviewed. The logs existed; the detection did not.
evidence: Field observation

Observed: After a breach, investigators find the attacker's logins in the VPN logs — collected for two years, never reviewed. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
What 'done' looks like

Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Explain the SIEM pipeline (2) Define initial detection use cases Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What turns log collection into detection?
choices: A. Collect more logs; volume is the answer.

B. A SIEM pipeline: centralized collection, normalized parsing, correlation rules and baselines that turn events into alerts, plus tuned use cases tied to attacker behaviors — logs are raw material, detection is the refinery.
C. Hire someone to read logs full-time; humans scale.
D. Logs are for forensics only; detection comes from antivirus.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the logs existed for two years. What was missing between 'collected' and 'detected'?
scenarios.why: Logs without analysis are write-only memory: the VPN logins sat for two years because no rule, baseline, or human ever evaluated them. A SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) centralizes logs, normalizes them into a common schema, and applies correlation (impossible-travel login: VPN from two countries in an hour), thresholds, and watchlists to generate alerts. But the SIEM is not magic — its value is its use cases (which attacker behaviors do we detect?) and their tuning. More logs (choice A) without use cases just grows the haystack; manual reading (choice C) does not scale past dozens of events.

scenarios.title: The 10,000 alerts
scenarios.situation: The SOC receives 10,000 alerts per day. Analysts cherry-pick the interesting ones; the rest auto-close. A real intrusion hid in the auto-closed pile for four months.
evidence: Field observation
Observed: The SOC receives 10,000 alerts per day. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
What 'done' looks like
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Triage alerts by tier (2) Tune detection rules Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct triage discipline?
choices: A. Hire more analysts to look at all 10,000.

B. Tune ruthlessly (kill noisy low-value rules, aggregate, whitelist known-good), tier alerts by severity with SLAs, automate enrichment and common closures with SOAR playbooks — the goal is fewer, higher-fidelity alerts, each with a defined response path.
C. Turn off alerting; the noise proves it does not work.
D. Auto-close faster so the queue looks clean.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the intrusion was IN the alerts. Why did no human evaluate it?
scenarios.why: Alert fatigue is a detection-system failure, not a staffing problem: 10,000 daily alerts means the rules are untuned, so analysts (rationally) ignore the queue — and the intrusion hides in the ignored mass. The fix is engineering the signal: measure precision per rule, disable or retune the noisy ones, aggregate related alerts into incidents, enrich automatically (asset criticality, threat intel, user context) so the analyst starts informed, and automate the deterministic closures (known-good scanner traffic) via SOAR. More analysts (choice A) scales the cost without fixing the precision; faster auto-close (choice D) hides the problem cosmetically.

scenarios.situation: Ransomware detonates at 2 AM. The on-call analyst has never seen it, improvises: pulls the wrong plugs, forgets to preserve logs, and notifies the wrong people. Containment takes 9 hours; evidence is trampled.

Observed: Ransomware detonates at 2 AM. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
What 'done' looks like

Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Write an incident playbook (2) Preserve evidence during containment Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What would a playbook have changed?
choices: A. Nothing — every incident is unique; playbooks are bureaucratic.

B. Everything: a ransomware playbook prescribes the first 60 minutes (isolate but do not power off, preserve memory/logs, engage IR lead, notify per the comms plan) — the analyst executes a rehearsed checklist instead of improvising at 2 AM, and evidence survives.
C. Playbooks replace analysts; the 2 AM call goes to the playbook.
D. The answer is better tools; process cannot fix 2 AM.
scenarios.hint: Hint: at 2 AM, with ransomware spreading, do you want the analyst INVENTING the response or EXECUTING it?
scenarios.why: Incidents are high-stress, low-frequency events — exactly when human judgment is worst and checklists are most valuable. The playbook encodes the hard-won lessons: isolate hosts from the network but do NOT power off (memory holds keys and artifacts; logs in RAM die with power), snapshot before reimaging, engage the defined roles (IR lead, legal, comms), and follow the notification matrix. The 9-hour improvisation becomes a 60-minute execution because the decisions were made calmly, in advance, and rehearsed in tabletops. Playbooks do not replace analysts (choice C) — they give analysts the first hour for free, so judgment applies to the novel parts.

scenarios.title: The IOC in the feed
scenarios.situation: The threat-intel feed flags an IP as malicious. An analyst blocks it everywhere immediately — including the IP of a critical SaaS provider that shares infrastructure. Outage for 400 users.
evidence: Field observation
Observed: The threat-intel feed flags an IP as malicious. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
What 'done' looks like
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Validate IOCs before acting (2) Tier response by confidence Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct threat-intel discipline?
choices: A. Threat intel is too dangerous; ignore the feeds.

B. Operationalize with context: validate IOCs (age, confidence, source reliability), check against your environment (is this IP in our allowlists/dependencies?) BEFORE blocking, and tier actions by confidence — intel informs decisions, it does not automate them blindly.
C. Block first, ask later — speed beats accuracy in security.
D. Only use free feeds; paid intel is a scam.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the feed said 'malicious IP'. What did the feed NOT know about your environment?
scenarios.why: Threat intelligence is information about adversaries (IOCs, TTPs, campaigns) — its value depends on relevance, timeliness, and confidence. Blocking on a raw feed IOC without validation caused the outage: shared infrastructure, CDN IPs, and stale IOCs make blind blocking self-inflicted DoS. The discipline: score IOCs (confidence, first/last seen, source), cross-reference your environment (dependency inventory, allowlists), and match action to confidence (high-confidence C2 -> block; medium -> alert; low -> watch). Intelinforms decisions, it does not automate them blindly.

scenarios.title: The breach nobody reported upward
scenarios.situation: An analyst finds evidence of data exfiltration on Tuesday but tells no one, 'investigating further.' By Friday it is a confirmed breach of 200K records — and leadership learns about it from a journalist.
evidence: Field observation

Observed: An analyst finds evidence of data exfiltration on Tuesday but tells no one, 'investigating further.' By Friday it is a confirmed breach of 200K records — and leadership learns about it from a journalist. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
What 'done' looks like

Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Define escalation triggers (2) Separate internal and external comms Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What communication discipline does incident response require?
choices: A. Analysts should fully confirm before telling anyone; premature escalation causes panic.

B. Defined escalation triggers and a comms plan: suspected exfiltration pages the IR lead immediately (hours, not days); leadership gets early heads-up with 'what we know / what we do not know'; legal and comms own external messaging. Bad news does not improve with age.
C. Keep incidents within the SOC; leadership does not need to know.
D. Notify customers first; they deserve to hear it immediately.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the journalist knew before leadership. What broke — the investigation, or the escalation?
scenarios.why: Incident communication has two audiences and two clocks: internal escalation must be fast (suspected exfiltration -> IR lead within the hour) because response options decay with time; external communication must be controlled (legal/comms own the message, regulators and customers get accurate, sequenced notifications). The analyst's instinct ('confirm first') is understandable and wrong: a 3-day silent investigation is how 'incident' becomes 'cover-up' in the postmortem and the press. The playbook defines triggers ('suspected exfiltration' is a trigger, not a conclusion) so escalation is procedural, not a judgment call at 2 AM. Customers (choice D) get notified per the legal/regulatory sequence — not first, not never.

scenarios.title: The SOC that measured tickets closed
scenarios.situation: The SOC reports '1,200 tickets closed this quarter' as its success metric. Dwell time is 120 days, and the same phishing template succeeds monthly. Leadership thinks security is fine.
evidence: Field observation

Observed: The SOC reports '1,200 tickets closed this quarter' as its success metric. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
What 'done' looks like
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Choose SOC outcome metrics Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What should the SOC actually measure?
choices: A. Tickets closed is fine; volume proves work.

B. Outcome metrics: MTTD (mean time to detect), MTTR (mean time to respond), dwell time, % of alerts tuned vs ignored, and repeat-incident rate — metrics that measure security outcomes, not activity. 'Tickets closed' rewards closing, not detecting.
C. Analyst hours worked; effort is the metric.
D. Number of tools deployed; coverage is the metric.
scenarios.hint: Hint: if every metric can improve while security gets worse, what are you measuring?
scenarios.why: Activity metrics (tickets closed, hours worked) measure busyness; outcome metrics measure security: MTTD (how fast you detect), MTTR (how fast you contain), dwell time (attacker freedom), and repeat rate (are lessons learned?). A SOC closing 1,200 tickets with 120-day dwell time is efficiently ignoring intrusions. Good metrics drive good behavior: MTTD/MTTR trending down means detection and response improve; repeat-incident rate exposes the phishing training gap the ticket count hid. Report the trend, not just the number — direction matters more than the absolute.

domains.name: Cloud Security
domains.description: Shared responsibility, cloud IAM, misconfiguration, data protection, and visibility — securing what you do not physically own.

scenarios.title: The open cloud storage bucket
scenarios.situation: A company migrates to the cloud and suffers a breach via a publicly readable storage bucket holding customer data. 'We thought the cloud provider secured it,' says leadership.
evidence: Field observation

Observed: A company migrates to the cloud and suffers a breach via a publicly readable storage bucket holding customer data. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
What 'done' looks like

Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Explain shared responsibility (2) Map controls per service model Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What does the shared responsibility model actually say?
choices: A. The provider secures everything; that is what 'cloud' means.

B. The provider secures OF the cloud (physical, hypervisor, network fabric); the customer secures IN the cloud (data, access, configuration) — the open bucket was the customer's configuration, and the model says so explicitly.
C. Responsibility is 50/50 on everything; both sides share blame.
D. The model only applies to IaaS, not SaaS.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the provider secured the storage SERVICE. Who configured the bucket?
scenarios.why: Every cloud provider publishes a shared-responsibility model with the same shape: the provider owns the infrastructure layers (buildings, hardware, virtualization, managed-service patching); the customer owns what they put in and how they configure it (data classification, IAM, bucket policies, encryption settings). The open bucket is the canonical customer-side failure — the provider secured the storage service; the customer configured it public. The line shifts by service model (IaaS: you own the OS; PaaS: provider owns the OS, you own the app and data; SaaS: you own data and access), but data and access are ALWAYS the customer's.

scenarios.title: The admin key in the repo
scenarios.situation: A developer commits a cloud admin access key to a public repo. Within hours, attackers spin up $80K of crypto miners. The key had full admin because 'it was easier than figuring out permissions.'
objectives: Apply least privilege in cloud IAM
evidence: Field observation

Observed: A developer commits a cloud admin access key to a public repo. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
What 'done' looks like

Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Apply least privilege in cloud IAM (2) Eliminate long-lived keys Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct cloud IAM practice?
choices: A. Keep one admin key and guard the repo better.

B. No long-lived keys for humans (SSO + short-lived roles), least-privilege policies (only the APIs the workload needs), no admin-by-default, key rotation and immediate revocation on exposure — and automated scanning for leaked keys. 'Easier permissions' is how $80K happens.
C. Longer keys; length defeats attackers.
D. Store the admin key in a private repo instead.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the miners needed ONE permission the app never used. What principle would have denied it?
scenarios.why: Cloud IAM failures are credential failures: long-lived admin keys are bearer tokens to the kingdom, and 'easier than permissions' concentrates maximum blast radius in the most-leaked artifact. The practice: humans authenticate via SSO and assume short-lived roles (minutes/hours, auto-expiring); workloads get IAM roles with only the APIs they call (the miner needed ec2:RunInstances — the app key should never have had it); policies start deny-by-default and add allows. Leaked-key scanning (in CI and in the provider's own detectors) plus one-click revocation bounds the damage when (not if) a secret escapes. A private repo (choice D) just moves the same admin key behind a thinner wall.

scenarios.title: The default-settings deployment
scenarios.situation: An engineer deploys a cloud database with default settings for a demo. Defaults include a public endpoint and no encryption. The demo becomes production; the database is breached in week three.
evidence: Field observation

Observed: An engineer deploys a cloud database with default settings for a demo. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
What 'done' looks like

Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Define hardened cloud baselines (2) Use CSPM for drift detection Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What practice prevents default-setting breaches?
choices: A. Nothing — defaults are the provider's responsibility.

B. Secure-by-default baselines enforced as code: infrastructure-as-code templates with hardened defaults (private endpoints, encryption on, logging on), peer review of infra changes, and continuous CSPM scanning that flags drift — the demo never gets public defaults because the template forbids them.
C. Ban demos; only production deployments allowed.
D. Change defaults manually after each deploy; checklists suffice.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the engineer did nothing wrong by the demo's standards. What made the demo's standards the problem?
scenarios.why: Cloud defaults optimize for 'it works in 5 minutes,' not for security: public endpoints, unencrypted storage, and open security groups are one demo away from production. The fix is making the secure path the easy path: IaC templates (Terraform/CloudFormation) whose defaults are hardened (private subnets, encryption at rest, access logging), so the demo inherits security instead of opting into it. CSPM (Cloud Security Posture Management) scanners then continuously audit the live environment against the baseline and flag drift — the week-three breach becomes a day-one finding. Manual checklists (choice D) fail under time pressure, which is exactly when demos become production.

scenarios.title: The unencrypted database snapshot
scenarios.situation: Database snapshots are shared with a partner account for analytics. The snapshots are unencrypted, and the partner's account is breached — customer data leaks from a copy the company forgot existed.
objectives: Protect data at rest in the cloud
evidence: Field observation

Observed: Database snapshots are shared with a partner account for analytics. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
What 'done' looks like
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Protect data at rest in the cloud (2) Govern snapshot sharing Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What data-protection discipline applies in the cloud?
choices: A. Trust partners; the sharing was the business need.

B. Encrypt everything at rest (KMS-managed keys), control snapshot sharing (encrypted snapshots, explicit grantee, time-limited), classify data BEFORE it lands in the cloud, and track copies — every copy is a new breach surface with the original's sensitivity.
C. Stop sharing data; analytics is not worth it.
D. Encryption is the provider's job; the snapshot inherited it.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the leak came from a COPY. What multiplies in the cloud without asking permission?
scenarios.why: In the cloud, data multiplies effortlessly: snapshots, replicas, backups, and shared copies each inherit the original's sensitivity but not always its protections. The discipline: encryption at rest by default (KMS keys you control, so you can revoke), snapshot sharing as a governed action (encrypted snapshots only, named grantees, purpose and expiry documented), and classification up front (you cannot protect what you have not labeled). The forgotten copy is the pattern — data lineage (knowing where copies live) is as important as the encryption. 'The provider encrypts' (choice D) is true for the default key but misses the point: the issue was sharing and lineage, not the cipher.

scenarios.title: The deleted logs
scenarios.situation: During an incident, investigators discover cloud audit logs were disabled 'to save costs' six months ago. The attacker's actions are unrecoverable — no record of what was accessed or changed.
evidence: Field observation

Observed: During an incident, investigators discover cloud audit logs were disabled 'to save costs' six months ago. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
What 'done' looks like

Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Require immutable audit logging (2) Alert on logging tampering Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What logging discipline does the cloud require?
choices: A. Logs are optional; cost savings justified it.

B. Non-negotiable audit logging: management-plane logs (who did what: CloudTrail equivalents) always on, immutable (no delete permissions for anyone, including admins), centralized, and retained per policy — logging is the cheapest incident-response tool and the first thing attackers disable.
C. Enable logs only during incidents; retroactive logging is fine.
D. Rely on the provider's internal logs; they will share them if asked.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the investigators needed to know 'who did what.' What is the ONLY source for that in the cloud?
scenarios.why: Cloud audit logs (CloudTrail, Azure Activity Log, GCP Audit Logs) record every management-plane action: who created the bucket, who changed the policy, who disabled the logging. They are the irreplaceable record — without them, the incident is uninvestigable, the blast radius unknowable, and the regulatory notification unwriteable. The discipline: always-on (no cost opt-out — the 'savings' bought blindness), immutable (dedicated log account, no delete rights, object lock), centralized (all accounts/regions to one place), retained (a year+ for forensics). Attackers disable logging first (choice B names why); 'enable during incidents' (choice C) is time travel.

scenarios.title: The SaaS nobody approved
scenarios.situation: A department bought a SaaS tool on a credit card, uploaded customer lists, and connected it to the company email. Security learns about it during the vendor's breach notification.
evidence: Field observation

Observed: A department bought a SaaS tool on a credit card, uploaded customer lists, and connected it to the company email. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
What 'done' looks like
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Discover and govern shadow IT Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct shadow-IT response?
choices: A. Ban all SaaS purchases; centralize everything.

B. Discover (CASB/browser/DNS visibility into unsanctioned apps), assess the found apps for data risk, bring the risky ones into governance (SSO, DLP, contract) or migrate off — and fix the WHY: make the approved path fast enough that shadow IT is unnecessary.
C. Ignore it; departments know their needs best.
D. Punish the department; fear prevents shadow IT.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the department solved a real business problem. What does banning teach them to do next time?
scenarios.why: Shadow IT is a symptom of friction: the approved path was too slow, so the business routed around security. Bans (choice A) and punishment (choice D) drive it underground — the next tool just will not be on a corporate card. The program: discover continuously (CASB, DNS logs, expense data reveal unsanctioned apps), triage by data risk (customer lists + email integration = high), and govern proportionally (SSO+MFA, DLP policies, data-processing terms for keepers; migration plan for the unacceptable). And fix the root cause: an approved SaaS request process measured in days, not months, removes the incentive to go rogue.

domains.name: CC Exam Strategy
domains.description: How the Certified in Cybersecurity exam works, where the points are, and the tactics that turn knowledge into a passing score.

scenarios.title: Walking in blind
scenarios.situation: A candidate sits for the CC exam knowing the domains but not the format — and burns 20 minutes on early questions, panics, and rushes the rest.
evidence: Field observation

Observed: A candidate sits for the CC exam knowing the domains but not the format — and burns 20 minutes on early questions, panics, and rushes the rest. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
What 'done' looks like
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Explain the CC exam format (2) Apply a pacing plan Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What should every candidate know before test day?
choices: A. Nothing about format matters; knowledge is all that counts.

B. The format: ~100 multiple-choice questions, ~2 hours, computer-based at a test center (or online proctored), pass/fail around 700/1000 — knowing the timing (about 1 minute per question) lets you pace, flag, and return instead of panicking.
C. The exam is adaptive; early questions matter more.
D. You can bring notes; it is open-book.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the candidate knew the material and still failed the clock. What preparation was missing?
scenarios.why: Format knowledge is free points: ~100 questions in ~120 minutes means roughly a minute per question — a pace you can feel. The strategy this enables: answer confidently-known questions fast (banking time), flag uncertain ones and move on (no 5-minute sinkholes), and return with remaining time. Panic comes from surprise; the candidate who rehearsed the timing treats question 80 like question 8. (Check current official details before your date — formats evolve; the principle of rehearsed pacing does not.)

scenarios.title: The 40-hour study plan
scenarios.situation: A candidate has 40 study hours. They spend 30 on cryptography math (their favorite) and 10 on everything else — then fail, having aced the crypto questions and bombed the heavily weighted principles and access-control domains.
evidence: Field observation
Observed: A candidate has 40 study hours. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
What 'done' looks like
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Allocate study by ROI (2) Recompute the plan from diagnostics Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct study allocation?
choices: A. Study favorites first; motivation matters most.

B. Weight effort by domain weight and personal weakness: allocate hours proportionally to exam-domain percentages, then shift toward your weakest areas within that — points per hour is the metric, not enjoyment per hour.
C. Study all domains equally; fairness is optimal.
D. Only study the hardest domain; easy ones take care of themselves.
scenarios.hint: Hint: 40 hours, five domains, different weights, different weaknesses. What maximizes expected points?
scenarios.why: Exams are point-maximization problems: an hour in a 25%-weighted weak domain earns more expected points than an hour in a 10%-weighted strong one. The method: get the official domain weights, take a diagnostic (this bootcamp's scenarios), rank domains by (weight x weakness), and allocate the 40 hours down that ranking. Favorites-first (choice A) feels productive and scores poorly; equal-split (choice C) ignores both weights and weaknesses. Recompute weekly: as weak domains improve, hours shift — the plan is a living allocation, not a fixed schedule.

scenarios.title: The 'BEST' question
scenarios.situation: A question asks for the BEST control against phishing. Two options are both correct-ish (training, email filtering). The candidate picks the first plausible one and moves on — wrong.
evidence: Field observation
Observed: A question asks for the BEST control against phishing. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
What 'done' looks like
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Parse qualifier words (2) Eliminate then select Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct way to read exam questions?
choices: A. Pick the first plausible answer; speed matters more than precision.

B. Read the FULL question stem (BEST/MOST/FIRST/NOT), eliminate clearly wrong options, compare the survivors against the question's exact ask, and choose the best fit — exam questions discriminate between good and best, and the stem tells you which.
C. Always pick the longest answer; detail indicates correctness.
D. Always pick 'all of the above' when present.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the question said BEST, not 'a valid.' What changes when the ask is superlative?
scenarios.why: CC questions (like most certification exams) are written to discriminate: several options may be defensible in isolation, but the stem asks for the BEST/FIRST/MOST appropriate — the option that best fits the scenario's constraints. 'Best control against phishing': training addresses the human, filtering addresses the vector — but MFA (if present) defeats credential theft even when the phish succeeds, making it the best technical control; the stem's scenario details decide. First-plausible (choice A) fails exactly these discriminators. The method is mechanical: read the stem twice, note the qualifier word, eliminate the clearly wrong, then argue the survivors against the qualifier.

scenarios.title: Thirty questions, twenty minutes
scenarios.situation: A candidate reaches question 70 with 20 minutes left — 30 questions remaining. Panic sets in; the last 30 are rushed, misread, and mostly wrong.
evidence: Field observation

Observed: A candidate reaches question 70 with 20 minutes left — 30 questions remaining. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
What 'done' looks like
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Execute a pacing plan (2) Triage under time pressure Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: How should time pressure be managed?
choices: A. Rush; speed is the only option left.

B. Prevent it structurally: the pacing plan (per-question budget, clock checks at quarters, 2-minute rule, flag-and-return) keeps this from happening — and if it does, triage: answer short questions first, eliminate-and-guess the rest, never leave blanks. Panic is a planning failure, not a character flaw.
C. Skip to the end and work backward; reverse order is calmer.
D. Close your eyes and guess all remaining; randomness is fair.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the crisis built up over 70 questions. When was the last chance to prevent it?
scenarios.why: The 70/20 crisis is a pacing failure with a structural fix: the per-question budget (~1 min), quarter clock checks (at 25/50/75 questions, verify time remaining), and the 2-minute rule (no sinkholes) prevent the deficit from accumulating. Flag-and-return is the mechanism: hard questions bank no time, they spend it — deferring them preserves the easy points. If the crisis still hits: triage ruthlessly — short/factual questions first (fast points), then eliminate-and-guess (never blank; there is no penalty for wrong answers on most such exams — verify current rules). Panic (choice A's rush) misreads questions; misreads are the most expensive errors because you knew the material.

scenarios.title: The night before
scenarios.situation: A candidate crams until 2 AM, arrives frazzled, forgets ID, and spends the first 20 minutes of the exam settling down. The score reflects the morning, not the knowledge.
evidence: Field observation

Observed: A candidate crams until 2 AM, arrives frazzled, forgets ID, and spends the first 20 minutes of the exam settling down. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
What 'done' looks like
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Prepare logistically for test day (2) Taper study correctly Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct test-day protocol?
choices: A. Cram all night; every extra fact helps.

B. Taper: light review two days out, normal sleep the night before, ID + confirmation + route ready the evening before, arrive early, and use the tutorial time to breathe and settle — the exam measures retrieval under pressure, and sleep, calm, and logistics are retrieval infrastructure.
C. Skip breakfast; nerves are fuel.
D. Learn new material the morning of; fresh is best.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the exam tests what you can RETRIEVE under pressure. What maximizes retrieval?
scenarios.why: Retrieval under pressure depends on sleep (memory consolidation), calm (working memory is anxiety's first casualty), and logistics (a forgotten ID or a late arrival spikes cortisol before question 1). The taper: stop new material 48 hours out (new facts crammed late interfere with organized recall), light review only, 8 hours of sleep, and a logistics checklist the night before (ID, confirmation, route, test-center rules). Arrive 30 minutes early; use the pre-exam tutorial minutes to settle breathing, not to cram. The all-nighter (choice A) trades a few fragile facts for degraded retrieval of everything else — a catastrophic trade.

scenarios.title: Pass or fail — next steps
scenarios.situation: The exam is over. The candidate either passed (now what?) or failed (now what?). Both outcomes need a plan; neither should be improvised in the emotional hour after.
evidence: Field observation
Observed: The exam is over. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
What 'done' looks like
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Plan post-exam steps Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What are the correct next steps for each outcome?
choices: A. Passed: frame the certificate and stop learning. Failed: give up; the exam is not for you.

B. Passed: claim the certification properly (ISC2 endorsement process, AMF dues, CPE plan — the cert is maintained, not owned), add it to the resume correctly, and keep building. Failed: get the domain score report, restudy the weakest domains (not everything), rebook after targeted prep — most passers failed something first.
C. Passed: immediately attempt a harder exam. Failed: retake tomorrow.
D. The result does not matter; certificates are meaningless.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the score report (pass or fail) is data. What does each outcome's data prescribe?
scenarios.why: Passing starts maintenance: ISC2 certifications require endorsement, annual maintenance fees, and Continuing Professional Education credits — the credential is a subscription to ongoing learning, and letting it lapse wastes the effort. Failing starts diagnosis: the score report breaks performance by domain — restudy the weak domains with targeted work (this bootcamp's diagnostic loop), not the whole syllabus, and rebook when the diagnostics say ready, not when the disappointment fades. Immediate retake (choice C) repeats the same preparation and the same result; the gap between attempts is where the passing happens.

domains.name: Start Here: ISC2 Certified in Cybersecurity
domains.description: Orientation for ISC2 Certified in Cybersecurity: how to use this bootcamp, how to study, and the assessment strategy that turns preparation into performance.

scenarios.title: Start Here: Your CC Bootcamp Tour
scenarios.situation: You have opened the Certified in Cybersecurity bootcamp: lessons, scenario drills, labs, and a mock exam. Without a plan it is a pile of content.
evidence: Guided path map
Work the bootcamp in this order: ISC2 Certified in Cybersecurity — core path. Each section assumes the previous one — jumping ahead is the fastest way to build shallow, fragile knowledge.
The study loop

For every domain: read the lesson (learn the concept), clear the scenario drills (apply it under no time pressure), complete the labs (do it hands-on), then prove it in the mock (timed, weakest-areas-first). Learners who skip the loop retain facts; learners who run it retain skill.
scenarios.prompt: What is the most effective way to work through it?
choices: A. Read everything top to bottom, then take the mock once.
B. Diagnostic first: run scenario drills across all domains to find weak areas, study those lessons hands-on, drill again, then take the mock under timed conditions — loop until the weak list clears.
C. Take the mock immediately; studying is for people who fail mocks.
D. Only do labs; lessons are optional.
scenarios.hint: Hint: what tells you where your study hours earn the most points?
scenarios.why: The diagnostic loop beats linear reading: scenarios reveal whether you can APPLY concepts (which is what the exam tests), lessons fill the exact gaps, re-drilling verifies. Reading everything first spends equal time on strong and weak areas; mock-only gives a score without building skill. Lessons build models, scenarios build exam judgment, labs build hands-on proof — the bootcamp works when all three feed the loop.

scenarios.title: How CC Candidates Actually Learn
scenarios.situation: Two candidates prepare: one memorizes definitions, the other works scenarios, explains concepts aloud, and does the labs. The memorizer freezes on scenario questions — which is most of the exam.
